strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored question: whether polynomial reducibility relations from theoretical CS can inform pretraining/fine-tuning strategies for transferable neural CO solvers. This is a novel conceptual bridge that could inspire future work on foundation models for CO.

The GCON-based single-task baseline is carefully validated with an ablation study (Table 2) against GCN, GIN, GATv2, and GFN, showing competitive or state-of-the-art results (e.g., new SOTA MaxClique on RB-small), lending credibility to the backbone used for subsequent transfer experiments.

The pairwise transferability experiments (Sec 4) are thorough and nuanced: multiple settings (frozen/reset, frozen/invert, fine-tune/invert) are tested for MIS<->MVC, and an extensive set of ablations (11 configurations) probe MIS->MaxClique transfer via distribution shift, global attention, and true reduction implementation, yielding genuinely informative negative and positive results.

The multi-task, leave-one-out experiments (Sec 5) provide a reasonably systematic empirical protocol for testing whether one related task in the pretraining set suffices for good transfer, and the final proposed 3-task pretraining backbone is empirically compared against meaningful baselines (20-epoch and 200-epoch single-task training).

The paper is transparent about mixed/negative results (e.g., MDS not benefiting from multi-task pretraining, frozen-backbone limitations, high variance in some transformer-augmented settings), which strengthens the honesty and credibility of the reported findings.
weaknesses: All experiments are conducted on a narrow set of graph distributions (RB-small and Barabasi-Albert-small) with no evaluation on larger or more diverse graph families (e.g., real-world graphs, larger synthetic benchmarks), which severely limits confidence that the observed transferability trends generalize beyond these specific small synthetic settings.

The central hypothesis linking 'computational reducibility' to 'transferability' is only loosely and post-hoc supported: the paper's own results show that theoretical equivalence (e.g., MIS/MVC duality) is insufficient on its own for transfer (Sec 4.1), and the task selection in Sec 5.2 for the pretraining backbone appears to be manually curated / partly result-driven (e.g., MDS included despite not fitting the reducibility-based expectation as cleanly) rather than derived from a predictive, testable theory, weakening the paper's core claimed contribution.

Statistical rigor is limited: most numbers are reported as mean ± std over only 3 or 5 runs with no significance testing, and several conclusions (e.g., 'almost always leads to faster convergence,' benefits of global message-passing in Exp #8-9) rely on small differences or single outlier runs (e.g., the one #9 run mentioned as an exception), making it hard to assess whether observed effects are robust.

The scope of transfer is restricted to only 6 closely related CO problems that largely already reside in the same 'linear orbit' per Filar et al.; it is unclear how the framework would extend to more distant problem families (e.g., routing, scheduling, or problems outside this orbit), limiting the paper's claimed relevance to 'foundation models for neural CO' more broadly.

Comparisons to the current strongest multi-task/foundation-model CO baselines (e.g., GOAL, UniCO, GFN-based multi-task variants) are absent from the empirical evaluation; the paper only compares against training-from-scratch baselines within its own framework, making it hard to judge how competitive the proposed transfer strategy is relative to existing multi-task neural CO solvers.

Fine-tuning budgets (20 epochs) versus pretraining/baseline budgets (200-700 epochs) create some asymmetries in the comparisons that, while acknowledged, make it harder to cleanly interpret whether gains stem from genuine transferable representations versus simply different training budgets and hyperparameter tuning per setting.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored question: whether theoretical notions of polynomial reducibility between NP-hard problems can inform practical transfer learning strategies for neural CO solvers.

The GCON-based encoder combined with energy-based (Ising/QUBO) loss functions achieves strong single-task performance, matching or beating several baselines (GCN, GIN, GATv2, GFN) on MVC, MaxClique, and MIS, including a reported new SOTA on MaxClique for RB-small graphs.

The experimental design is fairly systematic, progressing from pairwise transfer (MIS/MVC/MaxClique, motivated by known polynomial reductions) to multi-task pretraining/fine-tuning across six CO problems, with a reasonably thorough set of ablations (frozen vs. fine-tuned backbone, inverted output heads, graph transformer augmentation, true-reduction via complement graph).

The leave-one-out multi-task experiments provide some suggestive evidence that having at least one related task in the pretraining set is sufficient for fast, non-negative transfer, which is a useful empirical observation for designing pretraining task suites.

The paper is transparent about its own negative/mixed results (e.g., MVC→MIS not fully recovering baseline, frozen backbones failing on MaxClique under distribution shift), which is commendable rather than purely positive-result cherry-picking.
weaknesses: The central claim linking "computational reducibility" to transferability is largely post-hoc and qualitative rather than rigorously established: the paper picks three closely related problems with known polynomial reductions (MIS/MVC/MaxClique) and observes transfer, but reducibility is not quantitatively tied to any measurable transfer metric (e.g., no correlation analysis, no systematic test against pairs predicted to NOT transfer well by complexity theory). The claim in the abstract is thus considerably stronger than what the evidence supports.

Experiments are conducted on a narrow set of graph distributions (RB-small and BA-small only), raising concerns about generalizability of the transfer findings to other graph families or larger/more realistic instances typically used to benchmark neural CO solvers (e.g., SATLIB, real-world graphs, larger synthetic benchmarks).

Several core transfer results fall short of matching from-scratch baselines (e.g., Table 4 MIS→MaxClique transfers mostly underperform baseline; MVC→MIS converges to marginally worse performance), undermining the practical usefulness of the proposed pretraining strategy as a replacement for standard training, despite faster convergence.

The number of runs for many experiments is small (3 or 5), and some reported variances are large (e.g., Table 7 COLORING std of 21.84 for baseline), making it hard to assess statistical significance of many comparisons, especially in Sec 5 where conclusions about which tasks to include/exclude from pretraining rely on differences of similar magnitude to the noise.

The methodological contribution beyond the existing GCON architecture (Wenkel et al., 2025) and existing Ising-based losses (Lucas 2014; Sanokowski et al. 2024) is incremental: the main technical novelty is largely a different choice of loss function and task-transfer protocol (freeze/invert/fine-tune), rather than a new architecture or a theoretically grounded transfer mechanism.

The selection process for the final pretraining/fine-tuning task split in Sec. 5.2 is heuristic and somewhat circular — derived by manually inspecting earlier leave-one-out results and qualitatively reasoning about linear orbits — rather than following a principled, generalizable algorithm; it is unclear how this would scale to a larger set of CO tasks beyond the six studied, limiting the paper's claimed contribution toward 'foundational models.'

The connection to Filar et al.'s linear-orbit theory is used loosely to justify design choices (e.g., including K-coloring in pretraining because it is 'different') without rigorous theoretical or empirical validation that linear-orbit membership actually predicts transfer behavior quantitatively.

Limited comparison to other multi-task/foundation-model CO baselines (e.g., GOAL, UniCO) discussed in related work; no direct empirical comparison is provided against these alternative multi-task approaches, making it hard to assess the relative significance of the proposed approach.

The improvement over Wenkel et al. (2025) on MaxClique is attributed to loss function choice but the ablation supporting this (comparing MIS with quadratic vs Hamiltonian loss terms) is based on a single alternative setting and limited discussion, which is a relatively thin basis for the stated conclusion.

strengths: Novel and thought-provoking conceptual bridge between complexity-theoretic reducibility and empirical transfer learning for neural CO solvers, which is an underexplored angle relative to existing multi-task CO literature (RL- or SL-based generalist solvers).

Strong baseline construction: the GCON-based unsupervised solver matches or exceeds existing GNN baselines (GCN/GIN/GATv2/GFN) across MVC/MaxClique/MIS, including a reported new SOTA MaxClique result on RB-small, with a careful ablation isolating the effect of the loss function (Hamiltonian vs. Motzkin-Straus) from the GCON architecture choice.

The pairwise transferability experiments (Sec. 4) are methodologically thorough, testing multiple regimes (frozen/reset, frozen/inverted, fine-tuned/inverted, true-reduction via complement graph) and yielding a nuanced, honestly reported finding: theoretical equivalence (e.g., MIS/MVC duality) does not automatically guarantee successful representation transfer without backbone fine-tuning, and transfer across structurally dissimilar reduced graphs (MaxClique via complement) is harder and only partially successful.

The leave-one-out multi-task experiments (Sec. 5.1) provide a plausible and testable principle -- that having at least one 'reducible' task in the pretraining mix suffices for fast transfer even with a frozen backbone -- and this is used constructively to design a final pretraining/fine-tuning task split (Sec. 5.2) that approaches full single-task training performance using far fewer fine-tuning epochs.
Reasonable reproducibility signals: detailed problem/loss formulations (Table 1, Appendix A), explicit description of architecture/training choices, and a promised open-source implementation.
weaknesses: All experiments use small synthetic graph families (RB-small, BA-small); there is no evaluation on larger or real-world graphs, so it is unclear whether the transferability findings and the GCON backbone scale to graph sizes/domains typical of practical CO applications or of other neural CO benchmarks.

The central thesis linking reducibility to transferability remains largely qualitative/post hoc: the choice of the final 3-task pretraining set in Sec. 5.2 is justified by a sequence of heuristic arguments (task diversity, 'MDS shows little benefit,' K-coloring being in a different linear orbit) rather than a general, falsifiable rule; it is unclear how this selection procedure would scale or generalize to larger, more heterogeneous task families beyond the six studied here.

Several key quantitative claims are mixed or modest: e.g., in Table 2, GFN outperforms GCON on MIS (19.18 vs 18.12) and is close on MaxClique, undercutting the 'often comparable with SOTA' framing; similarly, several transfer settings in Sec. 4 (e.g., frozen-backbone MaxClique transfer, Exp #10) fail to approach baseline performance, and the paper's own conclusion is that the reducibility-transferability connection is 'not trivial' and needs further work, which tempers the significance of the central claim.

Statistical robustness is limited: most results are averaged over only 3-5 runs, and some reported differences (e.g., single outlier run beating baseline in Exp #9, Table 4) are highlighted as evidence despite high variance, which weakens the strength of the conclusions drawn from individual comparisons.

No wall-clock or parameter-efficiency accounting is provided beyond epoch counts; given that fine-tuning sometimes unfreezes the full backbone, it is unclear how much practical compute/time is actually saved compared to training from scratch, which is central to the paper's motivating claim about efficient transfer.

The scope of 'foundation model' aspirations is quite limited (6 related graph CO problems, all vertex/edge subset selection style tasks on unweighted undirected graphs); the paper does not test transfer to genuinely out-of-family tasks (e.g., TSP, weighted graphs, or problems outside the linear orbit framework) that would more convincingly support claims about generalizing toward a 'universal neural CO solver.'

strengths: Addresses a genuinely interesting and underexplored question: whether known polynomial reductions between NP-hard graph problems can inform practical neural transfer learning strategies, bridging theoretical CS and ML.

Comprehensive empirical study spanning pairwise transfer (MIS/MVC/MaxClique), leave-one-out multi-task transfer across six CO problems, and a full pretraining/fine-tuning backbone selection guided by reducibility theory.

Solid ablation validating the GCON backbone plus improved Hamiltonian-based loss functions against GCN/GIN/GATv2 and GFN baselines, with a careful explanation of why the improved loss outperforms the Motzkin-Straus-style loss used in prior work.

The appendix comparison between the proposed multi-task learning approach and a 'unified-task' SAT/reduction-chaining baseline is a valuable, well-motivated experiment that convincingly shows how graph blow-up from chained reductions degrades transferability, supporting the paper's design choices.

Extensive supplementary experiments (large graphs, size extrapolation, timing, zero-shot DIMACS evaluation) that, while not central to the main thesis, add robustness and transparency to the empirical claims.
Honest reporting of mixed/negative results (e.g., MVC→MIS not fully matching baseline, frozen-backbone failures under distribution shift) rather than only favorable outcomes.
weaknesses: The central thesis—that reducibility can 'inform' transferability—remains largely qualitative and heuristic; the actual guidance provided (e.g., 'include one related task,' 'maximize diversity') is intuitive rather than derived rigorously from the reducibility framework, and the paper's own conclusion ('these connections are not trivial and further work is needed') underscores the inconclusiveness of the core claim.

Absolute performance remains noticeably below optimal/Gurobi solutions (e.g., MVC 211.7 vs. true 206.95; MaxClique 16.9 vs. 19.07), and zero-shot DIMACS results are far from best-known solutions (e.g., MANN_a81: 300 vs. 1100), limiting the practical significance of the proposed transferable models.

Experiments are restricted to small synthetic random graph families (RB, BA) with at most ~1200 nodes; generalization to structurally diverse or larger real-world instances is only weakly assessed via zero-shot DIMACS results, which show large gaps to best-known solutions.

Several transfer settings show only marginal gains over baselines trained from scratch, or require access to the 'true' analytic reduction (e.g., explicitly constructing the complement graph for MaxClique) rather than the network discovering an equivalent mapping, which somewhat undercuts claims about learned representations capturing reducibility.
No empirical comparison to existing multi-task/generalist CO models (e.g., GOAL, UniCO, GFN-based multi-task approaches) despite discussing them in related work; only single-task GFN is benchmarked.
Statistical rigor is limited: no significance tests are reported despite substantial variance in several tables (e.g., high std for coloring results), making some comparative claims hard to verify.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not engage with any specific considerations (e.g., dual-use of optimization tools, environmental cost of extensive experiments), which is a missed opportunity for a paper with sizable appendix computational studies.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely interesting and underexplored question: whether polynomial reducibility between NP-hard problems can inform pretraining/transfer strategies for neural CO solvers, bridging theoretical CS and deep learning in a novel way.

The experimental scope is extensive: pairwise transfer (MIS/MVC/MaxClique), leave-one-out multi-task transfer, a curated 3-task pretraining backbone, size extrapolation, inference-time benchmarking, and zero-shot evaluation on real DIMACS instances, plus a thoughtful appendix comparing their multi-task approach against a 'unified-task'/SAT-reduction baseline that illustrates how reduction-induced graph blow-up harms transferability.

The GCON-based encoder with an improved Hamiltonian-based loss function shows competitive or superior performance versus several GNN/GFN baselines on standard CO tasks, lending some credibility to the backbone used in the transfer studies.

The discussion of why topology-preserving reductions (MIS/MVC) transfer more easily than topology-altering ones (MaxClique via complement graphs) is a reasonable mechanistic explanation and is empirically probed with several ablations (frozen vs fine-tuned, additional global attention, true reduction on complement graph).
weaknesses: Many of the central empirical claims are overstated relative to the actual numbers. For instance, Table 3 shows that fine-tuned MIS↔MVC models mostly fail to match or only marginally match baselines (e.g., MVC→MIS fine-tuned 18.00 vs baseline 18.12), yet the text describes this as 'remarkable' success; similarly in Table 4 most MaxClique transfer settings underperform the baseline, with only one run out of many beating it, but this is framed as 'convincingly demonstrating' transfer.

The connection between reducibility and transferability is ultimately qualitative and post-hoc rather than predictive. Task selection for the pretraining backbone in Section 5.2 relies on an ad hoc chain of heuristic judgments ('we believe,' 'sensible,' 'prefer') rather than a quantitative criterion derived from the reducibility theory being invoked, undermining the paper's central thesis that reducibility can systematically 'inform' transfer decisions.

Statistical support is thin: most results are averaged over only 3–5 runs with no significance testing, and several reported 'improvements' are within one standard deviation of baselines (e.g., Table 5 MaxClique/MDS, several entries in Table 7/11), making it hard to distinguish genuine transfer benefits from noise.

The work is evaluated only on synthetic random graphs (RB and BA models) of modest scale (hundreds to ~1200 nodes); there is no evaluation against strong existing multi-task/foundation-model baselines for CO (e.g., GOAL, UniCO, Sanokowski et al.'s diffusion model) on a shared benchmark, so the significance of the proposed transfer scheme relative to the state of the art remains unclear.

The architectural/methodological novelty is limited: the backbone (GCON) and overall unsupervised pipeline are taken essentially unchanged from Wenkel et al. (2025); the main technical change is a loss-function substitution, and the core contribution is an empirical study rather than a new algorithm or theory.

The paper's own conclusions are heavily hedged ('this relationship is not trivial,' 'further work is needed'), which, combined with mixed/negative results in several experiments (e.g., MDS showing no transfer benefit, frozen-backbone MaxClique transfer underperforming baselines), suggests the central research question posed in the title is not convincingly answered, limiting the paper's significance as a stand-alone contribution.

Important supporting analyses (the unified-task vs. MTL comparison, size extrapolation, DIMACS zero-shot results) are relegated to the appendix, while the main text's core pairwise and multi-task results are comparatively weaker, suggesting the paper's structure may be optimizing presentation rather than reflecting the true strength of evidence for its central claims.

strengths: Interesting and underexplored interdisciplinary framing connecting complexity-theoretic reducibility with neural transfer learning for combinatorial optimization, providing a principled (rather than purely ad hoc) rationale for pretraining task selection.

The GCON-based encoder with Hamiltonian/Ising-based unsupervised losses is a strong individual-task baseline, outperforming GCN/GIN/GATv2 and being competitive with GFN on MVC/MIS/MaxClique, lending credibility to the subsequent transfer experiments.

Extensive and carefully designed ablations in the pairwise transfer section (frozen vs. fine-tuned backbones, inverted head initialization, global message passing via graph transformer layers, true-reduction via complement-graph training) that probe multiple plausible mechanisms of transfer rather than a single simplistic comparison.

The multi-task leave-one-out and backbone-selection experiments (Sec. 5) offer a concrete, actionable methodology for selecting a small set of pretraining tasks that generalizes reasonably well to held-out tasks, which is relevant to building CO foundation models.

Appendix C's comparison between the proposed MTL approach and a 'unified-task' SAT/MDS-reduction baseline is a valuable addition, demonstrating a genuine limitation (graph blow-up and distribution shift) of naive full-reduction approaches that the paper's MTL method avoids.

Substantial supplementary experiments (large-graph MTL, size extrapolation, timing analysis, zero-shot DIMACS evaluation) add robustness and partially address generalization and reproducibility concerns.
Detailed hyperparameters and architecture tables (Appendix B) support reproducibility, and the authors state an open-source implementation will be provided.
weaknesses: The central question posed in the title/abstract -- whether reducibility can reliably inform transferability -- is only partially and inconsistently answered; the paper's own conclusion states the relationship 'is not trivial,' making the core contribution more exploratory than a crisp, well-supported finding.

Many fine-tuning results fall short of from-scratch baselines (e.g., most settings in Table 4, MVC->MIS in Table 3), and improvements are often marginal or within one standard deviation, weakening the strength of the transferability claims.

Results rely on a narrow problem set (6 classical graph CO problems) and only two synthetic graph families (RB, BA) of modest size (up to ~1200 nodes); it is unclear how well the reducibility-informed strategy would generalize to other CO problem classes (e.g., routing, scheduling) or substantially larger/real-world graphs.

No comparison is made against other multi-task/foundation-model baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., GOAL, UniCO, RL-based cross-problem methods), so the paper cannot position its empirical gains relative to competing multi-task neural CO approaches.

Statistical robustness is limited: most tables report only 3-5 runs, and some comparisons (e.g., Exp #9 in Table 4) rely on a single favorable run to support claims about variance/potential, which is weak evidence.

The selection of the final pretraining set (MDS, MIS, K-coloring) in Sec. 5.2 is justified by a mix of theoretical reduction arguments and post-hoc empirical observations (Table 6), making the procedure feel somewhat heuristic and not fully systematized or automatable for larger problem families.

DIMACS zero-shot results (Table 15) show large gaps to best-known solutions on several hard instances, tempering claims of strong out-of-distribution generalization despite being presented as encouraging.
